glance: The US and nine partners signed a declaration on protecting AI supply chains, and Sweden and the EU are expected to join next week. OpenAI let its agents pay at checkout, and analysts set expectations for SKF's spin-off Vertevo ahead of Tuesday's Capital Markets Day. Also in this edition: new open tools for building and browsing with agents, Tesla's Cybercab pricing, a court setback for JLR against BYD, in-line CT from ZEISS, and two studies on coatings and plain bearings.
brief: This is Vertical News. The United States and nine partners, including Japan, India and the UK, signed the San Francisco Declaration on Sunday. It commits them to protect the technology, materials and infrastructure behind advanced AI, and reports say Sweden, Germany, the Netherlands and the European Commission are expected to sign next week. OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet, which lets its agents buy things for users with single-use card tokens from Visa, Mastercard and American Express. And ahead of SKF Vertevo's Capital Markets Day on Tuesday, J.P. Morgan upgraded SKF to neutral, and Ålandsbanken valued the automotive spin-off at about ten billion kronor. The Nvidia scandal has spread to Washington, with questions about chip exports to China before results on Tuesday. Vercel released UI SDK, a set of accessible building blocks for coding agents, and Cloudflare open-sourced Kitesurf, a lightweight browser engine for agents. Researchers found more than twenty-four thousand apps built with Lovable exposing database records without a login. OpenAI and Databricks widened their partnership around governed company data. Tesla opened Cybercab orders at about thirty thousand dollars, plus two hundred and ninety-nine dollars a month for autonomy. A Dutch court lifted JLR's evidence seizure at BYD in the Defender lookalike case. ZEISS launched an in-line CT system that inspects up to ten battery cells a minute, and Marposs showed sensors that spot ten-micrometre chips on electrode cutting blades. In research, Hannover engineers used induction thermography to find one-micrometre cracks in hard coatings, and a Chinese study measured how load and oil temperature speed up seizure in sliding bearings.

stories.headline: US and nine partners sign the 'San Francisco Declaration' on AI supply chains; Sweden and the EU are expected to follow
stories.why: A US-led bloc on chips and AI technology is forming, and Swedish and EU membership would shape export controls and investment screening for European tech and automotive firms.
stories.source: US State Department · Poland Insight (citing FT)
body: The US State Department has published the San Francisco Declaration, signed at a retreat of its Pax Silica initiative on 15 November. The signatories are the US, Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, the UAE and the UK. The text states that "economic security is fundamental to national security" and commits members to protect sensitive technologies, materials and know-how in the supply chain for advanced AI from theft, illicit transfer and hostile takeovers, along with ports, energy and telecoms infrastructure.

The declaration proposes five working groups, covering innovation policy, adoption in key sectors, supply-chain cooperation, security hubs and resilience, plus coordinated responses to economic coercion. It is not legally binding and sets no deadlines. Citing the Financial Times, Poland Insight reports that Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands and the European Commission are expected to sign the following week. EU member states gave the Commission a negotiating mandate on 11 November, but Brussels has reservations about the AI provisions and wants to keep control of its own digital rules.
For European companies that buy chips or license AI technology, this could bring tighter screening of partners and investors, and new rules about where sensitive work is allowed to happen.

stories.headline: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet so its agents can pay for things on users' behalf
stories.why: Agent checkout has moved from demos onto real card networks, so product teams need a policy for how their sites treat buying agents.
body: OpenAI has introduced ChatGPT Wallet, which lets its personal agents, called dots, complete purchases for a user. The user saves a card once, asks a dot to find something, and approves each purchase with a security check. American Express, Mastercard and Visa are launch partners, and cardholders keep their usual rewards and protections.

The agent never handles the real card number. The card network issues a single-use payment token with its own number, code and expiry date. At launch the feature is limited to US Pro subscribers aged 18 or over, and OpenAI is not taking a commission on sales for now. It has published guidance to help merchants avoid blocking its agents. Not everyone is opening up: United Airlines plans to block agents from booking, and Amazon prevents them from buying on its site.

For product and UX teams this turns into concrete design work: whether to allow agents through checkout, how to show approval steps, and how to handle returns and fraud when the shopper is software acting for a person.

stories.headline: J.P. Morgan upgrades SKF and analysts put a value on Vertevo ahead of Tuesday's Capital Markets Day
stories.why: These estimates set the bar that SKF's automotive spin-off will be judged against when it presents its plans in Stockholm on 17 November.
body: J.P. Morgan raised SKF from underweight to neutral on Friday 13 November and lifted its price target from 250 to 300 Swedish kronor. The share closed around 281 kronor the day before, up almost 15% this year. The bank's base case values the remaining industrial SKF at 11.5 times 2027 operating profit and the automotive spin-off Vertevo at 7 times. It also expects 3.7% organic growth in 2027, below the 5.1% consensus. Separately, Ålandsbanken values Vertevo at about 10 billion kronor debt-free, or roughly 20 kronor per SKF share. It calls the targets reasonable but hard to reach given how the industry is structured.

Vertevo's stated targets are organic growth above the market, an adjusted operating margin above 6% in the medium term and at least 8% in the long term, ROCE of 10–15%, and net debt below one times EBITDA. SKF shareholders get one Vertevo share for every five SKF shares. The record date is 27 November, and trading on Nasdaq Stockholm starts on 1 December.
For OEM and supplier engineers, the Capital Markets Day should show how a stand-alone automotive bearing maker plans to fund EV and driveline products on margins this thin.

stories.headline: Nvidia scandal spreads into US chip-export politics as Trump heads to China
stories.why: Any tightening of US export policy after this week would affect the supply and price of AI hardware worldwide.
body: The fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia chief executive has reached Washington. Semafor reports that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under pressure over claims that he slowed restrictions on AI chip exports to China and left loopholes that let advanced chips reach the country indirectly. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says his department pushed for months to blacklist Megaspeed, a Singapore cloud company the US is investigating for alleged chip smuggling, but that decision belongs to Commerce.

Megaspeed told CNBC that Alice Huang, the executive at the centre of the reports, left in August 2025, and that it has hired outside counsel for an internal review. Lutnick is still due to travel with President Trump to meet Xi Jinping this week, and the White House says it has full confidence in him.
Nvidia reports quarterly results on Tuesday, its first under interim chief executive Colette Kress. Investors will watch for any guidance on China sales and on who will lead the company.

stories.headline: Vercel Labs open-sources UI SDK, a set of accessible interface behaviours for coding agents
stories.why: It addresses a common complaint about agent-written front ends, which is broken keyboard, focus and accessibility behaviour.
body: Vercel Labs has released UI SDK in public beta under the Apache 2.0 licence. It is a library of more than 50 'headless' behaviours with no styling of their own, such as popups, selection, typeahead, roving focus, reordering, drag-and-drop and virtualised lists. Adapters cover React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components. Focus handling, keyboard navigation and ARIA states are built in, and the core is described as aligned with WCAG 2.2 AA.

The release also includes an 'Agent Bridge' that lets AI agents operate an interface through MCP, using structured snapshots and actions instead of screenshots. Guardrails let developers allow or refuse agent actions on sensitive forms. Vercel says internal tests needed up to 69% fewer tool calls than DOM inspection, but that figure has not been checked independently. Stable React and Vue adapters are planned for early 2027.

For design-system teams, the idea is to give coding agents tested building blocks rather than letting them write interaction code from scratch. It also treats agents as a second kind of user that an interface has to serve.

stories.headline: Cloudflare open-sources Kitesurf, a lightweight browser engine built for AI agents
stories.why: More of a site's traffic will come from agent browsers that are not Chrome, and front-end teams will need to test for them.
body: Cloudflare has released Kitesurf under the Apache 2.0 licence. It is a browser engine that loads pages, runs JavaScript and renders them without Chromium or a browser container. It combines the Blitz layout engine and the Stylo CSS engine, runs scripts on Cloudflare's Dynamic Workers with the Boa engine as a fallback, and can output PDFs. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol, so tools like Puppeteer can connect, although not every feature works.

When Cloudflare first showed the engine in August, it reported three to seven times lower CPU and memory use than Chromium, for example about 58 MiB against 271 MiB per screenshot. Chromium still rendered about 1.7 times faster. Developers can run it locally, while hosting their own instance needs a paid Workers plan. Cloudflare calls it experimental.
For frontend developers, this adds another rendering engine that may visit their sites on behalf of users. Pages built on semantic HTML and standard layout are more likely to work in it.

stories.headline: Researchers find thousands of Lovable-built apps exposing personal data without a login
stories.why: Prototypes and internal tools from AI app builders need a security review before real customer data goes in.
body: Berlin security firm Crissy Field has published an English version of its study of 159,041 projects built with the AI app builder Lovable between December 2025 and September 2026. Of the 34,545 projects that used the Supabase database service, 24,664 sent database records to the browser as soon as the page loaded, with no login required. Follow-up read-only checks found email addresses on 7,403 of those sites. The authors say this should not be read as a confirmed leak rate.

Examples include a German lifestyle forum with more than 80,000 profiles and over 200,000 chat messages, ticket and food-sales records with addresses, and more than 1,000 records containing passport details. The report blames access-control mistakes in the database setup, which are easy to find at scale because many generated apps share the same patterns. No misuse has been reported.
For teams using AI builders, the lesson is to treat generated apps as untrusted until someone has checked database permissions and row-level security.

stories.headline: OpenAI and Databricks widen their partnership to connect ChatGPT and Codex to governed company data
stories.why: Enterprise AI is settling into a pairing of model provider and governed data platform, with spending controls per team becoming standard.
body: Databricks and OpenAI have extended the multi-year deal they signed in September 2025. OpenAI's GPT models, including the GPT-6 family and the open-weight gpt-oss, can now be called directly from SQL, notebooks and agents on Databricks. There are new plugins that bring Databricks' Genie analytics and a data-analyst tool into ChatGPT, and Codex gets a gateway tool, agent skills and a data-science plugin. A template for OpenAI's Agents SDK is available in Databricks Apps.

Through its Unity Gateway, engineering leaders can set budgets and track AI spending by team. No prices were given. Each company is also a customer of the other: Databricks says OpenAI is one of its largest customers, and Databricks engineers are getting Codex along with early access to new models.

For product leaders, the message is that the hard part of enterprise AI is now access to permissioned data and cost control, not the choice of model. Features that work inside a customer's existing data governance are easier to sell.

stories.headline: Tesla opens Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a $299 monthly autonomy subscription
stories.why: It is a live test of how regulators handle a production car designed around software instead of steering wheel and pedals.
body: Tesla has started taking orders for the Cybercab, its two-seat robotaxi with no steering wheel, pedals or side mirrors. At $29,990 it is about $7,000 cheaper than a Model 3, which makes it Tesla's cheapest car. Buyers must also subscribe to autonomous driving for $299 a month, with the first month free, which adds about $3,600 a year.

Sales are open only to selected customers at first, and the car will work only inside supported service areas, which Tesla has not named. The US safety regulator NHTSA is asking how Tesla concluded that the car meets federal safety standards. Without an exemption, federal rules allow a maker only 2,500 non-compliant vehicles a year. Zoox received an exemption for 5,000 vehicles over two years.

For engineers working on development and type approval, the open question is how a car without conventional controls gets certified. Europe will face the same question as UNECE rules for driverless vehicles take effect.

stories.headline: Dutch court lifts JLR's evidence seizure at BYD in the Defender lookalike dispute
stories.why: It is an early test of how far European OEMs can use EU courts to protect vehicle designs against Chinese competitors.
body: In August, a Dutch court allowed Jaguar Land Rover to have evidence seized at BYD's offices in Schiedam and Hoofddorp. JLR argues that BYD's Ti7 plug-in hybrid copies the Land Rover Defender. On 11 November the court in The Hague lifted the measure and ordered JLR to have the seized documents destroyed, with a penalty of 50,000 euros per hour of delay, capped at 500,000 euros. JLR must also pay BYD about 25,000 euros in legal costs.

The court found that the seizure was not needed to prove the alleged design-right breach. It also noted that the Ti7 is not yet on sale in the EU, so no harm was evident. Two cases are still open: one on EU design rights in The Hague and one on copyright and unfair imitation in Rotterdam. The Ti7 has a 300 kW system output and a 35.6 kWh battery, and goes on sale in the UK in January 2027 at £47,995, well below a seven-seat Defender.
The remaining cases will indicate how much protection design rights give OEMs as Chinese brands expand in Europe.

stories.headline: ZEISS launches INRADIA 3D, an in-line CT system that inspects up to 10 battery cells a minute
stories.why: CT is moving out of the lab and onto the production line, with AI making the pass/fail call, which matters for e-drive, battery and joining processes.
body: ZEISS has introduced INRADIA 3D, an automated computed tomography system designed to keep up with series-production cycle times. Unlike standard CT, where the part rotates, the X-ray source and detector move around a stationary part, while two robots take turns loading and unloading. ZEISS gives a throughput of up to ten prismatic battery cells per minute.

Scanning, reconstruction and analysis run in ZEISS INSPECT X-Ray with its Volume Inspection AI. Application-specific AI models decide pass or fail. The launch targets include electrode overhang, electrode count and folded electrodes in battery cells, soldered and welded joints in power electronics, and connector geometry. The system connects to manufacturing execution systems and handles calibration, temperature compensation and reference measurements automatically. ZEISS has not published resolution, X-ray voltage, price or availability.

For drivetrain and battery suppliers, inspecting every part with in-line CT would replace sample-based lab CT for internal defects. The open questions are how the AI pass/fail decisions are qualified and how they fit with existing NDT certification practice.

stories.headline: Marposs sensors spot 10-micrometre chips on battery-electrode cutting blades during production
stories.why: Condition monitoring of the tool itself, not only of the part, is reaching series production in cell manufacturing.
body: Marposs has presented an optical sensor system that watches the blades used to slit battery electrodes, in real time. The sensors sit in the blade holder or drive and detect edge chips as small as 10 micrometres. When damage passes a set threshold, the system can stop the machine within milliseconds or issue a warning, before damaged blades produce burrs that can later cause internal short circuits.

Readings are compensated for web speed and blade rotation to reduce false alarms, and the results were validated against manual inspection and microscopy. The system is in use on anode and cathode lines at an unnamed German cell maker. Marposs says it is ready for series production, can be retrofitted with minor changes and connects to manufacturing execution systems.

For test and quality engineers, it shows a pattern that also applies to bearing grinding and gear finishing: monitoring tool condition in-process to catch the cause of defects before parts need inspecting.

stories.headline: Induction thermography finds micro-cracks about one micrometre wide in hard WC-Co-Cr coatings
stories.why: It points to a contact-free way to find cracks in hard-coated or ground rolling surfaces such as rollers, bearing rings and gears.
stories.source: Journal of Nondestructive Evaluation (Leibniz Universität Hannover)
body: Researchers at the Institut für Werkstoffkunde, Leibniz Universität Hannover, tested induction thermography on a 400-micrometre sprayed tungsten-carbide coating on steel, both as-sprayed and ground. They created cracks by stretching specimens or by thermal shock, then heated the surface with a high-frequency induction coil and recorded it with an infrared camera at about 15 micrometres per pixel. Cracks disturb the heat flow, and Fourier phase analysis and principal component analysis bring them out. The paper is peer-reviewed and open access.

The method detected cracks about one micrometre wide on ground surfaces and below two micrometres as-sprayed, with clear signal-to-noise margins from strains of around 0.2%. A ferrite yoke worked better than a round coil, which has a blind spot at its centre, and two yoke orientations at right angles found cracks in all directions. The results matched dye-penetrant testing.

The work was motivated by calender rollers in battery-electrode production and so far uses only lab specimens, without a probability-of-detection study. Even so, it is a possible faster, chemical-free alternative to penetrant testing on hard rolling surfaces.

stories.headline: Rig tests show how load, speed and oil temperature drive wear and seizure in tri-metal sliding bearings
stories.why: It gives measured numbers on how long engine and driveline plain bearings survive oil starvation, which are useful for setting margins and checking simulations.
body: A team led by Dalian Maritime University, with Jiujiang Polytechnic University of Science and Technology, tested multilayer sliding bearings on a component-level rig with a 140 mm shaft. The bushes had a steel back, an aluminium-alloy layer, a nickel mesh and a lead-tin-copper overlay plated into grooves. Each factor was varied on its own in 12-hour wear tests, and in seizure tests the oil supply was cut off. The paper is peer-reviewed and published in Lubricants.

Raising the load from 10 to 25 MPa increased wear by about 74% and cut the time to seizure after oil cut-off from about 78 to 32 minutes. Higher speed reduced wear by about 43%, which fits a thicker oil film. Raising the oil temperature from 70 to 100 °C increased wear by about a third and shortened the time to seizure from about 52 to 31 minutes. After seizure, the groove structure had collapsed and only about a third of the overlay remained.
Because factors were tested one at a time, interactions are not captured, but the data is a useful reference for validating lubrication and wear models.

watch.title: SKF Vertevo Capital Markets Day, Tuesday
watch.text: Vertevo sets out its strategy in Stockholm on 17 November. Its shares start trading on Nasdaq Stockholm on 1 December.

watch.title: Sweden and the EU joining Pax Silica
watch.text: Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands and the Commission are expected to sign the declaration this week. The open questions are whether the EU gets carve-outs that protect its own digital rules, and how its reservations about the AI provisions are handled.

watch.title: Nvidia results and Anthropic's IPO
watch.text: Nvidia reports on 17 November, its first results under an interim CEO. Anthropic is expected to price its IPO midweek and start trading on Nasdaq on Thursday.
